analysis.one_liner: Cuts greenhouse gas emissions from federal public lands to net-zero by 2040, pausing new fossil fuel leasing and raising royalties to fund worker transition.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in December 2019 with 31 Democratic cosponsors, referred to three House committees, given a single hearing in February 2020, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Interior Department and Forest Service to cut greenhouse gas emissions tied to fossil fuels extracted from public lands—35% by 2025, 60% by 2030, 80% by 2035, and net-zero by 2040. It paused new coal, oil, and gas lease sales until the Interior Department certified that more leasing would not block those goals. It raised the royalty rate companies pay to drill and mine on federal land, added yearly per-acre fees on oil and gas leases, and put the money into a fund for cleanup, worker pensions and retraining, and economic development in fossil fuel dependent communities. It also required a public online dashboard of emissions and renewable energy production on federal lands.
analysis.who_benefits: People exposed to pollution from fossil fuel operations on public lands, since the bill required prioritizing reductions in environmental justice communities and barred actions that would increase co-pollutant emissions there [S3]. Communities and workers dependent on coal, oil, and gas extraction on federal land would receive transition money for remediation, pensions, wage support, severance, and retraining, funded by the new fees and royalties [S3]. The public would gain access to annual data on how much of each fossil fuel is produced on federal leases and how much gas is vented or flared [S3]. Future generations benefit from lower emissions tied to lands that produce roughly a quarter of U.S. fossil fuel emissions, per the USGS baseline the bill cites [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near federal fossil fuel operations and energy workers

how_it_helps.text: Imposes binding emission targets—35% below the 2014 baseline by 2025, 60% by 2030, 80% by 2035, and net-zero by 2040—covering both extraction and end-use combustion of fuels from public lands, with annual USGS verification and judicial enforcement if deadlines are missed.

Pauses new coal, oil, and gas lease sales for one year, and until Interior certifies further leasing is not inconsistent with net-zero emissions by 2040 and publishes a reduction strategy; if targets are missed, no new permits or lease sales are allowed until emissions fall back below target.
Raises the federal royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75% and adds a $4-per-acre annual fee on producing oil and gas leases and $6 per acre on nonproducing ones, indexing fees to inflation.

Creates a Federal Energy Transition Economic Development Assistance Fund distributing money for environmental remediation, worker pensions, wage bridges, severance, retraining, and local economic diversification, with prevailing-wage requirements and priority for displaced fossil fuel workers.

Requires a public dashboard showing fossil fuel production by type and state, the amount of gas vented, flared, or fugitively released, and renewable energy generated on public lands, updated annually in machine-readable form.
Requires the government to prioritize emission reductions affecting environmental justice communities and to ensure actions do not increase co-pollutant emissions in those communities.

analysis.who_pays: Coal, oil, and gas companies operating on federal lands and waters would pay higher royalties, new annual fees, and face a leasing pause and possible permit freezes when targets are missed [S3]. Some of those costs would likely reach consumers through higher fuel and electricity prices [general knowledge: production royalties and fees are typically passed through in commodity prices]. States and local economies that rely on federal energy revenues would lose leasing activity, though the bill returns half of the new royalty revenue to production states and directs fund money back to fossil fuel dependent communities [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil fuel producers on federal lands, partly consumers

drawbacks.text: The leasing pause and permit freezes could raise energy costs for consumers and cut revenue for states and counties that share in federal mineral royalties, particularly in the West, and the transition fund depends on revenue from the very leasing and production it curtails—so support for workers could shrink as production does.

Net-zero by 2040 including end-use combustion of fuels produced from public lands implies a near-total phase-out of federal fossil fuel production, a goal critics would call unrealistic on that timeline and one that could shift production to private or foreign lands with weaker environmental oversight, reducing U.S. emission benefits.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill paired its strictest-in-the-nation public lands emission targets with unusually detailed transition support—royalty increases, worker pension guarantees, remediation funding, and prevailing-wage rules—so the main costs fall on fossil fuel producers rather than directly on households. The honest caveats are real: energy prices could rise, fossil-fuel-dependent states would lose revenue, and the transition fund's own revenue source shrinks as the bill succeeds. But the drawbacks are transition costs, not flaws in the core design, and the bill's enforcement mechanisms (USGS verification, judicial review) gave it more teeth than typical climate framework bills.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Natural Resources, Agriculture, and Education and Labor committees, got one hearing in the Natural Resources Committee in February 2020, and never received a markup or floor vote before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Raúl Grijalva introduced the bill on December 16, 2019, with six original cosponsors including Reps. Haaland, DeGette, McEachin, Levin, Sablan, and Lowenthal.
It was referred to the Natural Resources Committee and additionally to Agriculture and Education and Labor, so three committees would each have had to act on parts of it.
In January 2020 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Conservation and Forestry, and the only recorded committee action afterward was a single hearing on February 26, 2020.
It gathered 31 Democratic cosponsors—no Republicans—and never advanced to a markup or a floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil, gas, and coal companies operating on federal lands came out ahead: no royalty increase, no new fees, and no leasing pause took effect, and federal leasing continued under the existing 12.5% royalty rate. States and counties receiving federal mineral revenues also kept the status quo.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal-lands fossil fuel producers and revenue-sharing states

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 31 cosponsors were Democrats, with no Republican support; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call breakdown exists.

industries.industry: Oil and gas companies on federal lands and waters
industries.note: The bill would have raised their royalty rate from 12.5% to 18.75%, added $4–$6 per-acre annual fees, paused new lease sales, and frozen permits when emission targets are missed. Its gain is the public's cost: it profits from leasing public minerals at below-market royalty rates while its combustion emissions are counted against the targets.

New federal coal lease sales would have been halted for at least a year and until Interior certified consistency with net-zero by 2040, with royalties also raised. Federal coal is among the most carbon-intensive fuels the bill targets.

The bill directs agencies to deploy renewable energy projects on public lands as a path to the targets and requires public reporting of solar, wind, and geothermal output on federal leases, expanding the opportunity set for clean energy on public acreage.

industries.industry: State and local governments receiving federal energy revenues
industries.note: They would lose leasing activity and the production tied to current royalty sharing, but gain a share of higher royalties (50% of new revenue returned to producing states) plus transition funds for remediation, worker support, and economic diversification.
The transition fund pays for abandoned mine reclamation, plugging orphaned wells, and land restoration, creating paid work with Davis-Bacon prevailing wages for firms and workers in those trades.
